articles.full_text:
HEAT exposure is unequal. Farmers, construction workers, street vendors and others whose jobs keep them outdoors may have little choice about when or where they work. Heat builds indoors in factories, warehouses and homes with poor ventilation. Informal workers have less access to shade, cooling, or social protection. When work stops, income may stop.
Children, older adults, pregnant people and those with chronic illnesses face heightened health risks. Many people live in poorly ventilated homes without reliable electricity and cooling.
Dr. Atsamon Limsakul’s presentation framed heat as a “socioeconomic risk” that reaches beyond individual discomfort. It cited 2.4 billion workers, nearly two-thirds of the global workforce, as being at risk from extreme heat. In 2024, the estimated loss was 639 billion work hours, with an economic cost of $1.09 trillion; the presentation reported that losses could reach $2.4 trillion by 2030.
Heat stress was estimated to have cost Southeast Asia the equivalent of 3.1 percent of working hours in 2015, or about 6.9 million full-time jobs. By 2030, the presentation projected a rise to 3.7 percent, roughly 13 million full-time jobs. It projected 2030 working-time losses of 7.8 percent in Cambodia, 6.4 percent in Thailand and 5.1 percent in Vietnam. Estimates of GDP losses from reduced labor productivity reached 5.5–6 percent by 2030 in several Southeast Asian countries.
For the Philippines, the presentation cited a projected GDP impact of 5.9 percent or $85 billion, based on cited economic analyses, not a guaranteed outcome. Still, it makes clear that the costs of heat can ripple through household income, business operations and national output.

Heat compounds existing inequalities. The presentation estimates that poor rural households lose 5 percent more income to heat stress than wealthier households. A worker paid by the day may have to choose between resting in dangerous conditions and losing wages needed for food, rent or loan payments. As Dr. Limsakul’s slides put it: “Heat creates an inequality multiplier.”
The response cannot be limited to telling individuals to drink water or stay indoors. Protection requires employers, governments, health services, communities and businesses to plan together.

My presentation used a simple disaster equation: Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability = Disaster. As I concluded: “We cannot control the climate pattern, but we can reduce avoidable harm by preparing early, sharing information clearly, and supporting the people most at risk.”
